### Supporting basis

`std::sort` is the superior choice because modern standard library implementations utilize Introsort, a hybrid algorithm combining QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort. This design guarantees O(n log n) worst-case performance, preventing the catastrophic O(n²) degradation that naive QuickSort suffers from on specific inputs. Furthermore, `std::sort` is heavily optimized by library maintainers for cache locality, branch prediction, and SIMD parallelism across diverse hardware architectures. Custom QuickSort implementations rarely match this level of low-level optimization. While your data from a uniform distribution reduces pivot-skew risks, the vast array size of 10,000,000 elements amplifies the cost of inefficient memory access patterns. `std::sort` minimizes these costs significantly better than a handmade solution, ensuring maximum throughput and consistent behavior regardless of edge-case data distributions.

### Recommendation

You should unequivocally choose `std::sort` for this task. Relying on a custom QuickSort introduces unnecessary maintenance burdens and performance ceilings that hinder scalability given the large dataset. The standard library function offers proven robustness and speed without the overhead of debugging custom recursion or pivot selection logic. Using built-in algorithms ensures your code remains portable, readable, and automatically benefits from future compiler and library upgrades. For millions of floating-point values, the marginal theoretical differences in average-case complexity are negligible compared to the practical advantages of highly tuned standard implementations. Therefore, `std::sort` is the most reliable and performant option for production-grade C++ code in this scenario.<|im_end|>
